They are 353 generated by bindgen from the C under `c/`, one module per link unit, and ship inside the 354 safe crate as its public `sys` module, with the C they bind: the published crate carries 355 the generated bindings, so that a dependent builds without bindgen or libclang, and the C 356 that remains, so that a dependent has the whole library and reaches what is not 357 translated yet through the raw bindings. How the safe crate uses them is 358 [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s; their lints and formatting are 359 [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Generated code section's. 360 361 ## 1. Layout 362 363 ```text 364 / 365 ├── Cargo.toml the safe crate's manifest; bindgen an optional build dependency 366 ├── build.rs builds or locates the C, compiles the C wrappers, regenerates on request 367 ├── c/ the C that remains, built into the crate 368 ├── sys// one link unit's bindings 369 │ ├── wrapper.h the headers they cover: the installed headers, and the internal headers its batches bind items of 370 │ ├── allowlist.txt one `function|type|var ` per line, filled by the batches 371 │ ├── external.txt the types other link units' bindings own, one regex per line 372 │ ├── shims.h 373 │ ├── shims.c the `crustify_` macro shims 374 │ ├── bindings.rs generated, committed 375 │ └── static_fns.c generated wrappers of the allowlisted `static inline` functions, committed 376 └── src/sys.rs the `sys` module: one public module per link unit, including its committed or regenerated bindings, or their doctest copy, and the re-exports of the types other link units own 377 ``` 378 379 Everything a build reads sits inside the crate, so that the packaged crate builds on its 380 own: no path leaves it, and `crustify/` is read only in campaign mode. 381 382 Within a link unit's Rust, `crate::sys::` is imported as `sys`, so that a raw 383 binding is `sys::`, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming section spells it. 384 The `sys` module is public: a consumer reaches the C that is not translated yet through 385 it, under its C names. It takes the place of the ecosystem's `-sys` crates, and is named after them. 386 387 `c/` is the C that remains: in a wrap campaign the whole source, and in a port campaign 388 the fork's `main`, which each switch trims of the module it ports, as 389 [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes. A build of 390 the crate therefore never holds both a module's C and the Rust that replaces it: the 391 remaining C reaches a ported module through the safe crate's exports, under their bare C 392 names, as the conventions' Exports section describes. 393 394 ## 2. Generation 395 396 The bindings follow from the headers at the `c/` revision, the allowlists, the generator 397 settings below, the bindgen version, pinned exactly in `Cargo.toml`, and the LLVM pinned 398 below, so that generating 399 twice from the same input gives the same bytes. The settings are the same for every 400 campaign: 401 402 - the output is formatted by bindgen's own formatter (`prettyplease`), never by the 403 toolchain's `rustfmt`, whose output differs between toolchains, so that a nightly build 404 regenerates the bytes a stable one committed; 405 - enums are generated as constants (`Consts`), without the enum name as a prefix, which 406 the safe types that bind them convert, as [`binding-types`](../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums 407 section describes; 408 - `Default` is derived, and layout tests are generated; 409 - C comments are kept as doc comments, and no doctest is collected from them, since they 410 hold C: the generated modules are modules of the safe crate, which rustdoc cannot exempt 411 one by one, so its doctests are collected from a copy of whichever bindings the build 412 uses, committed or regenerated, whose C comments are plain comments: the build script 413 writes it into `OUT_DIR`, and `src/sys.rs` includes it in their place under 414 `cfg(doctest)`; 415 - each allowlisted `static inline` function gets a compiled wrapper, `__extern`, in 416 `static_fns.c`, and is bound under its own name through 417 `#[link_name = "__extern"]`, so that it is called as an exported function is: 418 bindgen's `wrap_static_fns`; 419 - macro shims are bound like the functions they wrap; and 420 - an empty allowlist generates no item: `bindings.rs` holds only bindgen's banner, and 421 `static_fns.c` stays, empty, so that every link unit has both generated files. 422 423 An internal header's declarations are generated, and the wrappers of its `static inline` 424 functions compiled, as the link unit's own translation units see them: with the include 425 dirs and preprocessor definitions the build of the C a mode links records for them, its 426 generated headers and its out-of-tree libraries' include dirs among them, and the source 427 dirs taken from the checkout's `c/`. An item whose declaration depends on a definition that 428 differs between the variants is generated from the `plain` variant's configuration in every 429 mode, so that the committed bindings are those of every variant. 430 431 A type that another link unit's bindings own is blocklisted, as `external.txt` lists it, 432 and re-exported from that link unit's module under its C name, so that each C type has one 433 Rust type across the crate. A type an out-of-tree library's wrapper publishes is 434 re-exported as its wrapper's safe type, as 435 [`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes. 436 437 The bindings are generated for the campaign's target, the host's, as the setup workflow's 438 Builds section names it, the only target the crate supports: `src/sys.rs` fails to compile 439 on any other, naming it. 440 441 The C an out-of-tree library's wrapper bundles once its side campaign has ported part of 442 the library is compiled with its symbols prefixed, as 443 [`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Side campaigns section asks: 444 a generated header, force-included in every compile of that C and of its shims and 445 wrappers, renames each global symbol the library defines to `crustify__`, 446 and bindgen binds each item under its C name with the prefixed symbol as its `link_name`, 447 so that the Rust names stay C's. The crate passes the header's path to the C builds of the 448 crates that depend on it through its build script's metadata, under its `links` key, and 449 those force-include it too, so that their C calls the same copy. 450 451 The LLVM that generates the bindings, its libclang and the clang bindgen asks for the 452 system include dirs, is pinned with the bindgen version: its install prefix and version, in 453 the workspace manifest's `[workspace.metadata.crustify]`, as `bindgen-llvm` and 454 `bindgen-llvm-version`. Campaign mode generates with it 455 whatever drives the build, a sanitizer's or Miri's cargo driver included, which may name 456 another libclang of its own, and fails, naming both versions, when the pinned one is 457 missing or reports another version. A dependent's regeneration into `OUT_DIR`, compared 458 with nothing, takes the LLVM its host finds. 459 460 ## 3. Build modes 461 462 The build script runs in one of four modes: 463 464 | mode | when | C | 465 |---|---|---| 466 | bundled | by default, but for a wrapper whose `c/` is still its whole library | `c/`, built statically into `OUT_DIR` by the target's own build system, in the configuration of the `plain` variant | 467 | shared | the `shared` feature | `c/`, built as shared libraries into `OUT_DIR`, the same way | 468 | system | the `system` feature, and by default for a wrapper whose `c/` is still its whole library | an install, found through `_DIR`, then `pkg-config` | 469 | campaign | `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT` names a variant, or `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` a private build | the variant's build, recorded in `crustify/artifacts/build.json`: its static archive, when it records one, else its shared libraries | 470 471 The campaign's repository sets `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT` to `plain` in its 472 `.cargo/config.toml`, so that every build there runs in campaign mode unless the variable 473 names another variant, or is set empty to build as a dependent would. 474 475 In every mode, `shims.c` and `static_fns.c` are compiled against the headers the bindings 476 match, with the instrumentation of the C they link, and the bindings are the committed 477 ones unless the `bindgen` feature regenerates them into `OUT_DIR` from the headers of that 478 C. Campaign mode's tests and gates always regenerate them. 479 480 Bundled mode links the C statically, so that the bindings and the C they call always come 481 from the same revision; it sets no rpath. It builds `c/` against the out-of-tree libraries 482 its configuration uses as the target's build system finds them on the building host; a 483 dependent whose host lacks one supplies it through that build system's own search paths, 484 such as `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` and `PKG_CONFIG_PATH`. Shared mode leaves the remaining C's references 485 to ported modules undefined in its shared libraries, and the build script has the final 486 binary export what resolves them (`-Wl,--export-dynamic-symbol=` for each export), 487 as a cdylib already does; the libraries are found beside the binary, through an `$ORIGIN` 488 rpath, and ship with it. 489 490 System mode serves a crate whose `c/` is still the whole source: once a port campaign has 491 switched a module, an install of the library would hold that module's C beside the Rust 492 that replaces it, and the build fails, naming the switched modules. It checks the 493 version: the library found must be the one the bindings were generated from, as its build 494 system reports it (`pkg-config --modversion`), or, for an out-of-tree library's wrapper, a 495 release ABI-compatible with it, which shares its soname. Another version fails the build 496 with both versions named, unless the `bindgen` feature regenerates the bindings for it. Each link 497 unit's module exports the version the bindings match as `C_VERSION`. `_DIR` names an 498 install prefix: the build reads the headers under its `include/`, links the library under 499 its `lib/`, and takes the version from `lib/pkgconfig/.pc`. Without it, `pkg-config` 500 finds the library, which is linked as `pkg-config` resolves it, with no rpath. 501 502 An install carries neither the internal headers nor the functions its shared library does 503 not export, whichever header declares them, public or internal, and the shared libraries 504 shared mode builds lack the same functions, since the target's own configuration builds 505 them. Once the bindings reach either, system mode cannot serve the crate, nor shared mode 506 once they reach a function a shared library hides: the build fails in each, naming what 507 the library lacks, as system mode fails for a switched module, and bundled mode, whose 508 build in `OUT_DIR` has both, becomes the crate's default. The `bindgen` feature then regenerates from that build's 509 headers, never from an install's. 510 511 A link unit the target links as an executable, such as a command-line tool, has no 512 library. Bundled mode compiles its translation units as the target's build system records 513 them, without linking the executable, archives their objects and links the archive; 514 campaign mode links them from the variant's static archive, which holds them, as 515 [`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes; shared and system 516 modes, which link libraries, refuse its feature, naming the modes that serve it. An archive 517 member is linked only where one of its symbols is referenced, so a test that references 518 the translation unit defining the executable's `main`, directly or through another member 519 that references it, links a second `main` beside its harness's and fails to link. That 520 unit's other symbols are therefore ported to exports first, so that the members which 521 reference them stop pulling it in, and until then the units that pull it in are tested 522 through the variant's executable, run as a child process. 523 524 Campaign mode serves the campaign while it extends the bindings: batches add allowlist 525 entries and shims, and the bindings follow from them. It needs bindgen, which the safe 526 crate enables for its own tests through a dev-dependency on itself with the `bindgen` 527 feature, so that the campaign's tests and gates regenerate while dependents build from 528 the committed bindings. A build that does not enable the feature, such as the crate's 529 documentation, uses the committed bindings unchecked; the tests and gates always enable it. 530 The bindings it generates are compared with the committed ones: a difference fails the 531 build, naming the regenerated file, unless `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` is set, in which case 532 they are written over `bindings.rs` and `static_fns.c`. It links the C the variant built, 533 so that every test runs against the instrumented C it was built for. A variant that 534 records a `static` archive, as [`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section 535 describes, has it linked statically, with the libraries its shared library links, so that 536 the Rust reaches the internal functions the shared library does not export, and the 537 remaining C resolves the exports within the same link, as bundled mode's does; only the 538 out-of-tree libraries' installs of the same variant take an rpath. A variant that records 539 none has its shared libraries linked with an rpath to them, and the test binaries export 540 what the remaining C resolves to, as shared mode does. 541 542 No build links two copies of a module: a mode links either a module's C or the Rust that 543 replaces it, never both, and the Rust static library that the target's remaining C links 544 from a module's switch on carries no C of its own, as the porting workflow's Builds 545 section describes. 546 547 ## 4. Extending 548 549 The bindings grow with the batches: a batch whose items need a raw binding the bindings 550 lack extends its own link unit's input, and nothing else: 551 552 1. its link unit's `allowlist.txt` gains only the FFI items its items need, and 553 `wrapper.h` an internal header only when one of them is declared there; 554 2. a shim is added to `shims.h` and `shims.c` only for a macro whose expansion depends on 555 the build's configuration, as `crustify_`, as 556 [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes; 557 3. the bindings are regenerated, in campaign mode with `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` set; and 558 4. the safe crate is built and tested against them. 559 560 Where its link unit's headers name a type another link unit owns, the batch also extends 561 what the re-export needs, and only that: the type joins its own link unit's `external.txt`, 562 the owning link unit's `allowlist.txt` too while its bindings lack the type, and the link 563 unit's module in `src/sys.rs` re-exports it from the owner's, under its C name. 564 565 An allowlist or `wrapper.h` change alone leaves the C library as it is, so it reuses a 566 prebuilt variant; a shim compiles with the crate, as [Build modes](#3-build-modes) describes. 567 568 ## 5. Landing 569 570 A batch that changes an allowlist, `external.txt`, a shim or `wrapper.h` regenerates the 571 bindings and commits them in the same landing, so that the committed bindings always match 572 their input. The gates that check it, and that the crate packages, are 573 [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section's. 574 575 ## 6. Publishing 576 577 The safe crate is published with its raw bindings and the C it bundles. The packaged crate 578 holds the layout above, `src/`, the files of `c/` that the bundled build reads and the 579 C's license files, and nothing else of the repository but its README and the files the 580 package manager adds to every package, such as its manifest's original and its lockfile. 581

file.content: --- name: ffibox description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one." --- # ffibox ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a value; what C does not alias is plain Rust. Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md` describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes. What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there. ## Planning ### Dependencies › Adopted crates A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists, each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses. ## Binding workflow ### Binding workflow › Rust tree The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory. ## Binding and porting Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`, `docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too. ### Binding types A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them. ### Binding types › Safe layout While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox;`, and `CArc` for `FooArc`. A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address. Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::() != 0` and `!core::mem::needs_drop::()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its address, `FooBox` is `Box>` and a counted run of them `Vec>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align =`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with `Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions `CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box` and `Vec`. ## Testing ### Testing › UB tests The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test. ## Reviewing Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`. ### Reviewing › Objectives A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`, the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding. ### Reviewing › Reports A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is. --- name: ffimap description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), before planning an audit's worksets, and when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB." --- # ffimap ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them. It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document: ```bash ffimap > .json ``` Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs `from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`: ```bash ffimap --ffibox --sys-crates --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \ --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \ > .json ``` In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them, with `--regions`. Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features. Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts, or subtracted from it. `--sites ...` also lists where each named counter's increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named before it. The counters that recur: - `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in their signatures; - `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them; - `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`, `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows, slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change while they live; - `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread; - `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live reference; and - `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`. ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or `from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source. What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there. ## Binding and porting ### Binding › Safe boundary Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public `unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed. Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions, `code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included, which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and `.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved into its region. ## Accounting ### Accounting › Landing cells A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of the tree it lands. ### Accounting › API stability `ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the `::` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract [`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer: the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose `format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of the forms it defines: ```bash cargo + rustdoc -p --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json ffimap api diff .json .json --dep .json --items "" --format json ``` Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's unattributed public items, compared per module. ### Accounting › Records An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items. ## Reviewing ### Reviewing › Objectives A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters, and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and the types, trait impls and functions they name. - `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`. - `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated. - `ub`: these smells first, in this order: 1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions, `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`; 2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library does not allow what they assert; 3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or invalidates it; 4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored; 5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a reference, and outside a type's accessors; and 6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`. ## Audit ### Audit workflow › Worksets The audit's worksets are planned from a scan of the crate, run once each build configuration it audits is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of its objectives. A file outside every configuration scanned has no sites, and is planned from its source. For `ub`, the modules that hold the smells ffimap's review guidance lists for `ub` are reviewed first, in that order; for `contracts`, those that hold the crate's unsafe API and its justifications, the `contracts` counters above. The rest of the crate follows the smells. The modules are batched by their sites, and a module that is split keeps a type, trait impl or function with its sites in one batch. A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`, `.impl_clone`, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named `Drop for `, `Clone for `, `Send for ` or `Sync for `. Each review runs the same scan over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on. --- name: bindgen description: "How the raw bindings are laid out, generated, built in each mode, landed and published. Read before changing allowlists, shims, wrapper headers or build.rs, or scaffolding the bindings." --- # Raw bindings How a campaign's raw bindings are laid out, generated, built and shipped. They are generated by bindgen from the C under `c/`, one module per link unit, and ship inside the safe crate as its public `sys` module, with the C they bind: the published crate carries the generated bindings, so that a dependent builds without bindgen or libclang, and the C that remains, so that a dependent has the whole library and reaches what is not translated yet through the raw bindings. How the safe crate uses them is [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s; their lints and formatting are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Generated code section's. ## 1. Layout ```text / ├── Cargo.toml the safe crate's manifest; bindgen an optional build dependency ├── build.rs builds or locates the C, compiles the C wrappers, regenerates on request ├── c/ the C that remains, built into the crate ├── sys// one link unit's bindings │ ├── wrapper.h the headers they cover: the installed headers, and the internal headers its batches bind items of │ ├── allowlist.txt one `function|type|var ` per line, filled by the batches │ ├── external.txt the types other link units' bindings own, one regex per line │ ├── shims.h │ ├── shims.c the `crustify_` macro shims │ ├── bindings.rs generated, committed │ └── static_fns.c generated wrappers of the allowlisted `static inline` functions, committed └── src/sys.rs the `sys` module: one public module per link unit, including its committed or regenerated bindings, or their doctest copy, and the re-exports of the types other link units own ``` Everything a build reads sits inside the crate, so that the packaged crate builds on its own: no path leaves it, and `crustify/` is read only in campaign mode. Within a link unit's Rust, `crate::sys::` is imported as `sys`, so that a raw binding is `sys::`, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming section spells it. The `sys` module is public: a consumer reaches the C that is not translated yet through it, under its C names. It takes the place of the ecosystem's `-sys` crates, and is named after them. `c/` is the C that remains: in a wrap campaign the whole source, and in a port campaign the fork's `main`, which each switch trims of the module it ports, as [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes. A build of the crate therefore never holds both a module's C and the Rust that replaces it: the remaining C reaches a ported module through the safe crate's exports, under their bare C names, as the conventions' Exports section describes. ## 2. Generation The bindings follow from the headers at the `c/` revision, the allowlists, the generator settings below, the bindgen version, pinned exactly in `Cargo.toml`, and the LLVM pinned below, so that generating twice from the same input gives the same bytes. The settings are the same for every campaign: - the output is formatted by bindgen's own formatter (`prettyplease`), never by the toolchain's `rustfmt`, whose output differs between toolchains, so that a nightly build regenerates the bytes a stable one committed; - enums are generated as constants (`Consts`), without the enum name as a prefix, which the safe types that bind them convert, as [`binding-types`](../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums section describes; - `Default` is derived, and layout tests are generated; - C comments are kept as doc comments, and no doctest is collected from them, since they hold C: the generated modules are modules of the safe crate, which rustdoc cannot exempt one by one, so its doctests are collected from a copy of whichever bindings the build uses, committed or regenerated, whose C comments are plain comments: the build script writes it into `OUT_DIR`, and `src/sys.rs` includes it in their place under `cfg(doctest)`; - each allowlisted `static inline` function gets a compiled wrapper, `__extern`, in `static_fns.c`, and is bound under its own name through `#[link_name = "__extern"]`, so that it is called as an exported function is: bindgen's `wrap_static_fns`; - macro shims are bound like the functions they wrap; and - an empty allowlist generates no item: `bindings.rs` holds only bindgen's banner, and `static_fns.c` stays, empty, so that every link unit has both generated files. An internal header's declarations are generated, and the wrappers of its `static inline` functions compiled, as the link unit's own translation units see them: with the include dirs and preprocessor definitions the build of the C a mode links records for them, its generated headers and its out-of-tree libraries' include dirs among them, and the source dirs taken from the checkout's `c/`. An item whose declaration depends on a definition that differs between the variants is generated from the `plain` variant's configuration in every mode, so that the committed bindings are those of every variant. A type that another link unit's bindings own is blocklisted, as `external.txt` lists it, and re-exported from that link unit's module under its C name, so that each C type has one Rust type across the crate. A type an out-of-tree library's wrapper publishes is re-exported as its wrapper's safe type, as [`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes. The bindings are generated for the campaign's target, the host's, as the setup workflow's Builds section names it, the only target the crate supports: `src/sys.rs` fails to compile on any other, naming it. The C an out-of-tree library's wrapper bundles once its side campaign has ported part of the library is compiled with its symbols prefixed, as [`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Side campaigns section asks: a generated header, force-included in every compile of that C and of its shims and wrappers, renames each global symbol the library defines to `crustify__`, and bindgen binds each item under its C name with the prefixed symbol as its `link_name`, so that the Rust names stay C's. The crate passes the header's path to the C builds of the crates that depend on it through its build script's metadata, under its `links` key, and those force-include it too, so that their C calls the same copy. The LLVM that generates the bindings, its libclang and the clang bindgen asks for the system include dirs, is pinned with the bindgen version: its install prefix and version, in the workspace manifest's `[workspace.metadata.crustify]`, as `bindgen-llvm` and `bindgen-llvm-version`. Campaign mode generates with it whatever drives the build, a sanitizer's or Miri's cargo driver included, which may name another libclang of its own, and fails, naming both versions, when the pinned one is missing or reports another version. A dependent's regeneration into `OUT_DIR`, compared with nothing, takes the LLVM its host finds. ## 3. Build modes The build script runs in one of four modes: | mode | when | C | |---|---|---| | bundled | by default, but for a wrapper whose `c/` is still its whole library | `c/`, built statically into `OUT_DIR` by the target's own build system, in the configuration of the `plain` variant | | shared | the `shared` feature | `c/`, built as shared libraries into `OUT_DIR`, the same way | | system | the `system` feature, and by default for a wrapper whose `c/` is still its whole library | an install, found through `_DIR`, then `pkg-config` | | campaign | `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT` names a variant, or `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` a private build | the variant's build, recorded in `crustify/artifacts/build.json`: its static archive, when it records one, else its shared libraries | The campaign's repository sets `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT` to `plain` in its `.cargo/config.toml`, so that every build there runs in campaign mode unless the variable names another variant, or is set empty to build as a dependent would. In every mode, `shims.c` and `static_fns.c` are compiled against the headers the bindings match, with the instrumentation of the C they link, and the bindings are the committed ones unless the `bindgen` feature regenerates them into `OUT_DIR` from the headers of that C. Campaign mode's tests and gates always regenerate them. Bundled mode links the C statically, so that the bindings and the C they call always come from the same revision; it sets no rpath. It builds `c/` against the out-of-tree libraries its configuration uses as the target's build system finds them on the building host; a dependent whose host lacks one supplies it through that build system's own search paths, such as `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` and `PKG_CONFIG_PATH`. Shared mode leaves the remaining C's references to ported modules undefined in its shared libraries, and the build script has the final binary export what resolves them (`-Wl,--export-dynamic-symbol=` for each export), as a cdylib already does; the libraries are found beside the binary, through an `$ORIGIN` rpath, and ship with it. System mode serves a crate whose `c/` is still the whole source: once a port campaign has switched a module, an install of the library would hold that module's C beside the Rust that replaces it, and the build fails, naming the switched modules. It checks the version: the library found must be the one the bindings were generated from, as its build system reports it (`pkg-config --modversion`), or, for an out-of-tree library's wrapper, a release ABI-compatible with it, which shares its soname. Another version fails the build with both versions named, unless the `bindgen` feature regenerates the bindings for it. Each link unit's module exports the version the bindings match as `C_VERSION`. `_DIR` names an install prefix: the build reads the headers under its `include/`, links the library under its `lib/`, and takes the version from `lib/pkgconfig/.pc`. Without it, `pkg-config` finds the library, which is linked as `pkg-config` resolves it, with no rpath. An install carries neither the internal headers nor the functions its shared library does not export, whichever header declares them, public or internal, and the shared libraries shared mode builds lack the same functions, since the target's own configuration builds them. Once the bindings reach either, system mode cannot serve the crate, nor shared mode once they reach a function a shared library hides: the build fails in each, naming what the library lacks, as system mode fails for a switched module, and bundled mode, whose build in `OUT_DIR` has both, becomes the crate's default. The `bindgen` feature then regenerates from that build's headers, never from an install's. A link unit the target links as an executable, such as a command-line tool, has no library. Bundled mode compiles its translation units as the target's build system records them, without linking the executable, archives their objects and links the archive; campaign mode links them from the variant's static archive, which holds them, as [`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes; shared and system modes, which link libraries, refuse its feature, naming the modes that serve it. An archive member is linked only where one of its symbols is referenced, so a test that references the translation unit defining the executable's `main`, directly or through another member that references it, links a second `main` beside its harness's and fails to link. That unit's other symbols are therefore ported to exports first, so that the members which reference them stop pulling it in, and until then the units that pull it in are tested through the variant's executable, run as a child process. Campaign mode serves the campaign while it extends the bindings: batches add allowlist entries and shims, and the bindings follow from them. It needs bindgen, which the safe crate enables for its own tests through a dev-dependency on itself with the `bindgen` feature, so that the campaign's tests and gates regenerate while dependents build from the committed bindings. A build that does not enable the feature, such as the crate's documentation, uses the committed bindings unchecked; the tests and gates always enable it. The bindings it generates are compared with the committed ones: a difference fails the build, naming the regenerated file, unless `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` is set, in which case they are written over `bindings.rs` and `static_fns.c`. It links the C the variant built, so that every test runs against the instrumented C it was built for. A variant that records a `static` archive, as [`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes, has it linked statically, with the libraries its shared library links, so that the Rust reaches the internal functions the shared library does not export, and the remaining C resolves the exports within the same link, as bundled mode's does; only the out-of-tree libraries' installs of the same variant take an rpath. A variant that records none has its shared libraries linked with an rpath to them, and the test binaries export what the remaining C resolves to, as shared mode does. No build links two copies of a module: a mode links either a module's C or the Rust that replaces it, never both, and the Rust static library that the target's remaining C links from a module's switch on carries no C of its own, as the porting workflow's Builds section describes. ## 4. Extending The bindings grow with the batches: a batch whose items need a raw binding the bindings lack extends its own link unit's input, and nothing else: 1. its link unit's `allowlist.txt` gains only the FFI items its items need, and `wrapper.h` an internal header only when one of them is declared there; 2. a shim is added to `shims.h` and `shims.c` only for a macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration, as `crustify_`, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes; 3. the bindings are regenerated, in campaign mode with `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` set; and 4. the safe crate is built and tested against them. Where its link unit's headers name a type another link unit owns, the batch also extends what the re-export needs, and only that: the type joins its own link unit's `external.txt`, the owning link unit's `allowlist.txt` too while its bindings lack the type, and the link unit's module in `src/sys.rs` re-exports it from the owner's, under its C name. An allowlist or `wrapper.h` change alone leaves the C library as it is, so it reuses a prebuilt variant; a shim compiles with the crate, as [Build modes](#3-build-modes) describes. ## 5. Landing A batch that changes an allowlist, `external.txt`, a shim or `wrapper.h` regenerates the bindings and commits them in the same landing, so that the committed bindings always match their input. The gates that check it, and that the crate packages, are [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section's. ## 6. Publishing The safe crate is published with its raw bindings and the C it bundles. The packaged crate holds the layout above, `src/`, the files of `c/` that the bundled build reads and the C's license files, and nothing else of the repository but its README and the files the package manager adds to every package, such as its manifest's original and its lockfile.

# Mandatory questions

## Campaign

1. **Which repository and revision should this campaign use?** (`id: source`)
   - Answer: `https://sourceware.org/git/glibc.git`, `glibc-2.39` (`ef321e23c2`): the
     `c/` submodule. The release the parent campaign, `crustify-rs/ffmpeg-bindings`, links:
     the system's glibc, package `libc6-dev 2.39-0ubuntu8.9`, whose distribution patches
     `crustify/artifacts/dependencies.json` of the parent records. Side campaign of
     `crustify-rs/ffmpeg-bindings` and of `crustify-rs/libgit2-bindings`, which links the
     same glibc 2.39.

2. **Should this campaign port the C implementation to Rust, or create safe
   Rust wrappers?** (`id: campaign`)
   - Answer: `wrap`

3. **What should this campaign target: a named subset of modules, or a named
   subset of functions and types, or the whole target repo? You can define them
   now or we can brainstorm them during the live session. You can also let the
   orchestrator decide.** (`id: scope`)
   - Answer: what the parent campaigns consume from libc, the entities their dependency
     records count: for `crustify-rs/ffmpeg-bindings`, `struct tm` (`libavutil/bprint.c`,
     `libavutil/parseutils.c`) and `FILE` (`libavformat/dump.c`); for
     `crustify-rs/libgit2-bindings`, 871 functions, 95 structs and 2 globals, counted per
     module over its 168 modules that use libc; growing as the parents' waves need more

4. **Which model and billing should do the translation work?**
   (`id: translate-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5`, the parent
     `libgit2-crustify`'s answer since 2026-11-13, in the current template's format:
     `<claude | codex>, <subscription | api>[, proxy: openrouter][, args: ...]`
   - Format: `<provider/model, api | subscription>`, e.g.
     `openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5, api`. The provider is the first
     segment and selects both the billing rate table and the backend CLI.
     Supported providers:
     - `anthropic/<model>` — Anthropic direct, driven by Claude Code;
     - `openai/<model>` — OpenAI direct, driven by Codex;
     - `openrouter/<vendor>/<model>` — OpenRouter, which resells every vendor
       behind one key, so the vendor segment picks the CLI: `anthropic/*` is
       driven by Claude Code and everything else by Codex. OpenRouter
       supports `api` billing only.

5. **Do you want agentic review after translated work lands? If so, which
   model and billing should perform each review?** (`id: review-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5`, after each wave

6. **Should I run fully autonomously end to end?** (`id: autonomy`)
   - Answer: `no`

# Optional questions

Unanswered optional questions use their defaults.

## Campaign execution

7. **Which model and billing should plan the campaign, and how many planner runs
   should it make? Each run emits what the plan lacks and corrects what the runs
   before it committed.** (`id: plan-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5, runs: 1` for an
     advance that names its entities; the parent's answer otherwise.
   - By default: the translation model and billing, 2 runs.

8. **Should the campaign use the default batching and parallelism settings, or
   customize them?** (`id: workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`, the parent's answer.

9. **What batch caps should review agents use? We recommend the same caps as
   translation by default.** (`id: review-workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`, the parent's answer.

10. **Which objectives should review agents review for? By default, every one the
    reviewer offers.** (`id: review-objectives`)
    - Answer: `all`
    - Without `fix`, reviewers report and reproduce what they find but patch nothing.

11. **Which sanitizers should the campaign build and test under? By default, every one
    the toolchain supports.** (`id: sanitizers`)
    - Answer: `asan-ubsan, tsan, bsan`, instrumenting the Rust; the system's glibc they
      link is not instrumented. MSan is not built.
    - From 2026-11-13, as in the parent: BSan runs over the whole workspace, and as a
      regression gate, only once before each ship point; otherwise an agent may run it on
      small things, the tests its own work adds or changes and a review's reproducer,
      each test named and under a `timeout`. This departs from the `testing-gates`
      skill's Regressions section.
    - Miri needs no build and is always on.

12. **How should the target be configured: which of its build features should be
    enabled or disabled?** (`id: target-config`)
    - Answer: none: libc is the system's, which the parent and every other library on
      the host link, so glibc is not built; `c/` is its source, for reading its behaviour,
      and the raw bindings are generated from the host's headers.
    - By default: the target's default configuration, with deprecated features disabled.

## Commits

13. **Which git identity should the campaign's commits carry: an author, and any
    co-authors? By default, Crustify's own, `crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the
    GitHub account `crustify-ai`), as the author, with no co-author.** (`id: identity`)
    - Answer: `author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>, co-authors: crustify
      <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the GitHub account `crustify-ai`)

## Autonomy (if question 6 is answered `no`)

Answer these approval-gate questions only if question 6 is answered `no`.

14. **Should I wait for your approval before starting the setup phase?** (`id: gates.setup`)
    - Answer: `no`
15. **Should I wait for your approval before starting the translation phase?**
    (`id: gates.translation`)
    - Answer: `no`, the parent's answer
16. **Should I wait for your approval between modules?** (`id: gates.module`)
    - Answer: `no`
17. **Should I wait for your approval before starting review passes?** (`id: gates.review`)
    - Answer: `no`

# Benchmark recording questions

18. **Where and in what format should the dashboard be recorded?** (`id: dashboard`)
    - Answer: `<repo-checkout>/crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md`, `standard` template

# Additional instructions

Unless otherwise stated, preserve the format of the dashboard exactly.

# Wave 3's write through a shared stream handle takes the stream's lock itself

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-2/batch-0/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer): a correction
to a campaign artifact the planner owns, proposed.

## Signal

A plan that would ask a later batch for a binding its analysis cannot make sound
(`evolution` §2, "plan corrections"). Planner run 1 (`25b3fe2`) plans `fprintf` (wave 3) as
`fprintf(stream, "%s", message)` through `_IO_FILE`'s shared handle, on the ground that
"glibc locks every stream operation, which the binder confirms before a shared handle
writes". Wave 2's analysis does not confirm it for every stream:

- `vfprintf` (`c/stdio-common/vfprintf-internal.c:1540-1563`) locks with the
  `_IO_flockfile` macro, which `c/libio/libio.h:282` makes a no-op when the stream carries
  `_IO_USER_LOCK`. `__fsetlocking(fp, FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER)` sets that flag
  (`c/libio/__fsetlocking.c:31-32`). Native code, not Rust, sets it.
- `flockfile` (`c/stdio-common/flockfile.c`) takes the stream's lock (`_IO_lock_lock`) with
  no flag check, and the lock is recursive (`sysdeps/nptl/stdio-lock.h`: owner and count).
  So `fprintf` called inside `flockfile`/`funlockfile` is serialized whatever the stream's
  locking mode.

`File`'s `Sync` (`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`, wave 2) therefore rests on this rule: every
operation bound on `FileRef` holds the stream's lock, taken with `flockfile`, for the
whole of its access. A `Sync` that relied on the stream's locking mode would rest on data
the native code can change, which `binding`'s Safe boundary section forbids.

## Destination

A campaign artifact: `modules.json` and `schedule.json`, the planner's. `flockfile` and
`funlockfile` (`stdio-common/flockfile.c`, `stdio-common/funlockfile.c`, declared in
`libio/stdio.h`) join the plan ahead of wave 3, or in its batch, since wave 3's `fprintf`
binding needs them. They could also be bound privately inside `fprintf`'s module, as the
lock its one call takes, with no public API of their own.

## Change

Planner run 2 adds the two functions as items wave 3 reaches. The fixed-arity form stays
as planned: `flockfile(stream)`, `fprintf(stream, "%s", message)`, `funlockfile(stream)`,
with the count returned, or `errno`'s `io::Error` on a negative return.

## Validation

None yet. Wave 3's binder confirms it from `fprintf`'s analysis.

## Review

Not reviewed.

# Wave 3's write through a shared stream handle takes the stream's lock itself

Status: `open`. Filed by glibc-crustify `wave-2/batch-0/run-1` (2026-11-13), under the
default `repair` autonomy (`crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` gives no `evolution` answer): a correction
to a campaign artifact the planner owns, proposed.

## Signal

A plan that would ask a later batch for a binding its analysis cannot make sound
(`evolution` §2, "plan corrections"). Planner run 1 (`25b3fe2`) plans `fprintf` (wave 3) as
`fprintf(stream, "%s", message)` through `_IO_FILE`'s shared handle, on the ground that
"glibc locks every stream operation, which the binder confirms before a shared handle
writes". Wave 2's analysis does not confirm it for every stream:

- `vfprintf` (`c/stdio-common/vfprintf-internal.c:1540-1563`) locks with the
  `_IO_flockfile` macro, which `c/libio/libio.h:282` makes a no-op when the stream carries
  `_IO_USER_LOCK`. `__fsetlocking(fp, FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER)` sets that flag
  (`c/libio/__fsetlocking.c:31-32`). Native code, not Rust, sets it.
- `flockfile` (`c/stdio-common/flockfile.c`) takes the stream's lock (`_IO_lock_lock`) with
  no flag check, and the lock is recursive (`sysdeps/nptl/stdio-lock.h`: owner and count).
  So `fprintf` called inside `flockfile`/`funlockfile` is serialized whatever the stream's
  locking mode.

`File`'s `Sync` (`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`, wave 2) therefore rests on this rule: every
operation bound on `FileRef` holds the stream's lock, taken with `flockfile`, for the
whole of its access. A `Sync` that relied on the stream's locking mode would rest on data
the native code can change, which `binding`'s Safe boundary section forbids.

## Destination

A campaign artifact: `modules.json` and `schedule.json`, the planner's. `flockfile` and
`funlockfile` (`stdio-common/flockfile.c`, `stdio-common/funlockfile.c`, declared in
`libio/stdio.h`) join the plan ahead of wave 3, or in its batch, since wave 3's `fprintf`
binding needs them. They could also be bound privately inside `fprintf`'s module, as the
lock its one call takes, with no public API of their own.

## Change

Planner run 2 adds the two functions as items wave 3 reaches. The fixed-arity form stays
as planned: `flockfile(stream)`, `fprintf(stream, "%s", message)`, `funlockfile(stream)`,
with the count returned, or `errno`'s `io::Error` on a negative return.

## Validation

None yet. Wave 3's binder confirms it from `fprintf`'s analysis.

## Review

Not reviewed.

---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Setup

### Setup › Provisioning

CodeQL and wavefront's query pack dependencies are installed, as its README describes.
`crustify/.gitignore` lists `wavefront/codeql` and `wavefront/.cache`.

### Setup › Artifact tree

`crustify/wavefront/` is scaffolded for wavefront's state.

### Setup › Baseline

Once the builds and the baseline are recorded, the CodeQL database is created from a
traced build of the `plain` configuration in a fresh scratch dir, with `c/` as its source
root, and its T1/T2 tables are extracted, through a bootstrap configuration in
`crustify/tmp/`; the campaign's own configuration is the plan's.

## Planning

Planning reads `docs/scoping.md`, `docs/graph.md`, `docs/batching.md`,
`docs/type-lifecycle.md`, `docs/artifacts/t3.md` and `docs/artifacts/schedule.md`.

### Decomposition › Runs

Each planner run brings the configuration and the T3 tables up to date with the plan: it
emits what is missing, migrates what follows an earlier wavefront schema, adds what the
scope adds and corrects what is wrong. A changed configuration or T3 row changes the graph,
so the `todo` waves whose batches it moves are re-planned, and the `depends_on` in
`modules.json` when it moves them.

### Decomposition › Dependencies

The configuration's `modules` are authored from `modules.json`: each module's files, with
the entities its `items` list select, each by the kind it is in C. Wavefront refuses an
entry that claims what its file only declares, and a unit two modules claim, so that every
entity is owned by exactly one module; the configuration is verified against the CLI.
<!-- TODO: wavefront makes a unit of every macro an installed header defines, but of an
internal header's macro only where the closure's code expands it, so an internal API macro
no C of the closure expands is planned nowhere, and it makes units of the configuration and
attribute macros the closure expands too. It has yet to make units of the macros that are
API, and only those, count enums and
macros in the modules' records, and tell a closed enum from a flags one, which the planner
judges until then, as `scheduling`'s Later stages section describes. -->

A module's dependency records are counted from a schedule of the whole closure, without
`schedule_seeds`: its module record's `depends_on` gives its in-tree records, with their
`unique_edges` and `total_edges`; its items give the `counters`, and their references
whose `scope` is `external` the out-of-tree records.

### Decomposition › Foundational modules

The foundational modules' candidates are selected from the configuration's graph, after
the T3 tables are written, so that their cast edges resolve type-erased values: the
type-erased units that no cast edge ties to a named type, and the units whose pointers
carry the `string` property, that depend on no other module's types. Each candidate's body
is read before it is admitted. Each member's lifecycle role is identified as
`docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes and submitted to the ownership store, so that the bindings of
the foundational modules find it.

### Scheduling › Order

The link units and modules are ordered from the configuration, after its T3 tables are
written, and reviewed there:

- every type-erased parameter and field with no cast, followed until it is read as a named
  type, stored, returned or lost. A hop that dispatches on a tag and reads different types
  per branch establishes none of them;
- every cast edge wavefront derives between two public types, each that is no type
  relation dropped;
- every public type in a cast relation, the pairs that are a hierarchy recorded as
  `base_derived` rows; and
- the type-minting macros, the source checked for invocations that conditional
  compilation hides from the traced build.

## Batches

### Versioning › Lifecycle › Batches

The CodeQL database and tables under `crustify/wavefront/codeql/`, and wavefront's
`.cache`, are gitignored state every batch needs: they are symlinked into each batch's
worktree once it is forked.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->
